questions.question: When will quantum computers actually be useful?

hybrid.answer:
Quantum computers are already starting to be useful in a limited way, a first clear quantum advantage is expected in 2026, and the big transformational impact comes by 2030.

- **Today:** On current machines we can already start simulating small molecules [1]. The errors aren't fully corrected but can be mitigated, so the scaling is still exponential, only a slower exponential, and you can get value already today with this architecture [2].
- **2026:** At IBM, our roadmap points to the first provable quantum advantage on some application by 2026 [3]. That means a real application on real systems that can't be done with classical computing alone [4].
- **By 2030:** At IBM, we expect the first fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2030 [5]. That is when the real transformational power arrives [6]. It is about this decade, not 10 to 40 years away [7].

The first areas I expect are simulating nature (chemistry, catalysis, materials), global optimization, and finding hidden structure in small but complex data sets [4]. In finance, even a 1% better optimization would matter a lot [8]. I'd rate this roadmap as credible because we have kept to it year by year since 2016 [4].

questions.question: Should banks be worried about quantum computers breaking encryption?

hybrid.answer:
Yes, banks should act now, and I'd say we are already late. Once we reach fault-tolerant quantum computing, the public-key (asymmetric) cryptography that secures internet connections, digital signatures and secure data transmission will be attacked and stop working [1]. At IBM, our roadmap targets the first fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2030, so the impact is a matter of this decade, not 20 to 40 years away [2].

**Why waiting is risky**
- Solutions to move to something secure against quantum attacks already exist, but you have to start now rather than wait and hope it only becomes a problem in 30 years [3].
- Someone is already collecting encrypted data that circulates on the internet and storing it. Once quantum machines are available, they can go back, read it and even forge digital signatures and contracts [4].

**What I'd do**
- Move now in a way that also prepares you for future changes. Nobody can guarantee that today's quantum-safe algorithms will stay secure forever [5].
- Build in crypto agility, so you can migrate from one cryptographic scheme to another easily. We will have to do it anyway, so why not now [6].

questions.question: What about the energy cost of all this AI?

hybrid.answer:
My view is that the energy cost depends on how we build the models: many smaller specialized models are far better than one giant model for everything.

- **The single giant model:** It could bring many discoveries by connecting data of different types, but it would be hugely expensive, especially in use, since a model is trained once and used a million times [1]. Using a model with 1,000 trillion parameters just to decide where to go to dinner makes no sense [1]. Training energy also doesn't scale linearly with model size, but at least quadratically [1].
- **The better way:** Build many models, each around one trillion parameters or fewer, specialized by task, modality or use case, with an orchestrator on top, which can itself be an AI model, that calls the right ones and integrates the answers [2]. Because the cost grows with the square of size, the sum of smaller models costs much less than the one big model [2]. Done right, this can use an order of magnitude less energy and be more accurate [2].
- **Accuracy:** Mixing too many uncorrelated things in one model can produce nonsensical answers, since these models only learn sequences and predict the next step [3].

I also push for base models to be built once, in the open and collaboratively, so people don't redo the same models with lots of compute and CO2 emissions to reach the same result [4].
